d.title: The join family, by what it does with an unmatched row
d.caption: Every one of them is the same cross product filtered by the ON condition. They differ in one decision only: what to do with a row that found no partner — drop it, or keep it padded with NULLs.

d.title: Predicting the row count, on the shop tables
d.caption: Every count here was produced by running the query. The rule behind all of them: a left row contributes one output row per partner it has — and, under an outer join, one row when it has none.
cells: one per order, direction is irrelevant
one per line item, not per order

d.title: The same filter, in WHERE and in ON
d.caption: Both queries are valid and one of them answers a different question. In WHERE the filter runs on the joined rows, so Mara's padded row — whose status is NULL — fails the test and disappears. In ON it decides which orders *pair* with a customer, and the outer join still keeps everyone.

d.title: Three counts on Iker's one padded row
d.caption: Iker has a single row after the LEFT JOIN and no order in it. `COUNT(*)` answers 'how many rows did the join make for him', which is never below one. `COUNT(o.order_id)` answers the question the report asked.

d.title: Four ways to ask 'has at least one order'
d.caption: The first three return the same seven customers. The fourth is not a semi join at all — it returns one row per order, and the DISTINCT that usually follows it exists only to undo the multiplication the join just created.

d.title: Four ways to ask 'has no order', and which survive a NULL
d.caption: All four return Iker and Mara **today**, because `orders.customer_id` happens to be NOT NULL. `NOT IN` returns nothing the day that subquery yields a single NULL — so the two that are correct by construction are the two to write.

d.title: 'The latest order per customer' is not an aggregate
d.caption: The question asks for a **row** chosen by an ordering, not a value computed over a group. There is no aggregate that returns 'the status on the row where placed_at was the maximum', and MAX on each column separately silently mixes rows: Chen's MAX(status) is `refunded`, from a different order than his MAX(placed_at).

d.title: Subtotals without three queries
d.caption: A report that wants per-country, per-tier and overall totals is one query, not three. The subtotal rows carry NULL in the column that was rolled up — which is indistinguishable from a real NULL until `GROUPING()` tells you which is which.

d.title: FILTER, and the CASE it replaces
d.caption: They compute the same number. FILTER says what it means in the order you would say it out loud, and it applies to any aggregate — including the ones where a CASE inside would change the result rather than restrict it.

d.title: The four set operations
d.caption: `UNION` is `UNION ALL` plus a de-duplication you did not ask for: it sorts or hashes every row to find repeats, which costs time and quietly removes rows that were legitimately identical. Reach for `UNION ALL` and add the `DISTINCT` only when you mean it.

d.title: How a set operation pairs the columns
d.caption: The pairing is by **position**, never by name. Two queries that both select a name and a country will line up silently wrong if one of them lists them in the other order — and it only errors when the types happen to disagree.
